paras: The manhunt for Will Jones was a posse pursuit with bloodhounds near Tunica, Mississippi, in late August 1910, after Jones, a Black farm employee, was accused of trying to pull a nine-year-old white girl through her bedroom window. Dispatches said he had been located and that a lynching was feared if he was caught, but no report of his capture or fate was found.
Laura Thomas was the daughter of C. W. Thomas, who lived at Bostick's Mill, about six miles southeast of Tunica, and Jones was described as one of the Black men employed by her father.

According to a Tunica dispatch in the Hattiesburg News, Jones cut the wire screen on the girl's bedroom window on Monday night, reached through and grabbed her. Her mother seized the child, and for a few minutes the two struggled with the man over her until the screams brought white men from the place and he ran. The same dispatch said that a check found every other Black worker on the place asleep, which made Jones the suspect, and that bloodhounds were brought from Memphis and put on his trail.

A shorter dispatch in the Pensacola Journal, datelined August 24, put the attempt on Tuesday instead, called the charge an allegation, and said the screams drew 'a large crowd' that began the chase at once. Both reports said Jones had been located, and the Pensacola version added that he would likely be 'summarily dealt with if apprehended.'
No report of Jones's capture, arrest, lynching or trial appears in the coverage, which ends with the posse still on his trail.

The story ran only in the white press, first as wire dispatches on August 25 under headlines such as 'Hounds and Posse on Trail of Negro.' A syndicated feature carried in Kentucky the next day under the headline 'Girl Rescued From Negro' called Jones a 'fiend' and 'the brute' and told the story from the mother's rescue. A shortened version without Jones's name or the pursuit then circulated in 'Mississippi News' columns in papers at Oxford, Port Gibson, Starkville, Grenada, Macon, Leakesville and Brookhaven between September 1 and 3. Apart from the Pensacola Journal's 'it is alleged,' the reports gave the accusation as fact and mentioned the expected lynching without comment; no Black-press coverage was found.
The two dispatches differ on the day: the Hattiesburg News said Monday night, about August 22, while the Pensacola Journal said Tuesday, about August 23.

reader.title: Manhunt for Will Jones
bases: A posse with bloodhounds hunted Will Jones, a Black man accused of trying to pull a white girl through a window, and the Tunica dispatches said a lynching or summary punishment was feared if he was caught (A1, A2); no killing or capture is reported, so this is at most a threatened lynching.
Two differently worded Tunica dispatches (A1, A2) and a syndicated feature (A3) agree on the accusation, the chase and the bloodhound pursuit, though all carry the accusers' account.

accounts.label: Tunica dispatches
accounts.gist: A man identified as Will Jones cut a window screen and tried to drag Laura Thomas out; white men drove him off and a posse with bloodhounds trailed him; lynching was feared if he was caught.

accounts.label: Syndicated feature
accounts.gist: A dramatized version naming Jones as one of Thomas's employees and saying bloodhounds had trailed and located him; the later Mississippi briefs drop his name and the pursuit.

framing.detail: Reports took the accusation as fact (except A2's 'it is alleged'), called Jones a 'fiend' and 'the brute', and treated a lynching as a foreseeable result without objection.

conflicts.note: Neither dispatch is clearly better; A2's dateline (Aug. 24) is earlier, A1's (Aug. 25) is from a Mississippi paper.
